posts.title: How to Protect Your Money From Online Fraud in India: A Practical Guide
posts.excerpt: Most scams use the same few tricks. Here is how to spot them, how to protect your money, and exactly what to do if you have already lost some.
posts.meta_title: Online Fraud in India: How to Protect Your Money
posts.meta_desc: Online fraud in India follows a few repeating patterns. Learn the warning signs, three simple rules, and what to do in the first hour after a scam.
posts.cover_alt: Community members at an Aagahi Foundation session on online fraud in India and cyber safety
posts.author: Aagahi Foundation

faqs.q: Can I get my money back after an online scam?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but nobody can promise it. Your best chance comes from acting fast. Call 1930, report on cybercrime.gov.in, and tell your bank straight away so it can try to hold the money before it moves on.

faqs.q: Does my bank ever ask for my OTP or PIN?
faqs.a: No genuine bank employee needs your OTP, card PIN, CVV or UPI PIN. If someone asks, treat the call as a scam, even if the caller knows your name or account number.

faqs.q: I only want to receive money by UPI. Do I need to enter my PIN?
faqs.a: No. You enter your UPI PIN only to send money. If a request says you must enter your PIN to receive money, it is a trick, so decline it.

faqs.q: What is Chakshu?
faqs.a: Chakshu is a facility on the Sanchar Saathi portal of the Department of Telecommunications. You can report suspicious calls, SMS or WhatsApp messages that you received in the last 30 days. It is for suspected fraud, not for money you have already lost.

faqs.q: How can I help my parents or grandparents stay safe?
faqs.a: Sit with them once and walk through the three rules in this guide. Agree on one family phone number they can call before they act on any urgent request. A two-minute call to a relative stops many scams.

posts.content:
Online fraud in India costs families real savings every week, and it rarely looks like a scam at first. It looks like a call from your bank, a message about a parcel, or a friendly stranger offering part-time work. The good news is that most scams follow the same few patterns. Once you know them, you can stop almost all of them.

At Aagahi Foundation, we run financial literacy and cyber safety sessions for community members and for police personnel. This guide puts the most useful points into plain language. Share it with someone who does not use the internet much. They need it most.

Five patterns behind most online fraud in India

Scammers change their story, but the structure stays the same. They create a reason to panic or a reason to hope, and then they ask you to act quickly.

  1. The KYC or bank call. Someone says your account will be blocked today unless you "update KYC". They ask for an OTP or a PIN, or they ask you to install an app.
  2. The UPI "collect" trick. You are told money is on its way. Then a request arrives and you are asked to enter your PIN to "receive" it. That one step sends money out.
  3. The fake helpline. You search for a customer care number and click the first result. Scammers sometimes get their own numbers to show up there.
  4. The easy-money offer. Part-time jobs, "tasks" for rewards and guaranteed investment returns all work the same way. A small payout builds trust, and then the big payment disappears.
  5. The fake officer. A caller claims to be from the police, customs or an investigation agency. They say you are under "digital arrest" and must stay on a video call. No real agency arrests anyone over a video call.

Three rules that stop most scams

You do not need technical skill to stay safe. You need a few habits that you follow every time.

Rule 1: Never share an OTP, PIN or CVV

These codes exist so that only you can approve a payment. Your bank, a delivery company or a government office has no reason to ask for them. Government guidance on UPI says the same: share your card number, expiry date, CVV, PIN or OTP with no one. Remember that a UPI PIN is only for sending money.

Rule 2: Pause when someone is in a hurry

Fraud depends on speed. So slow down on purpose. Say "I will call you back" and hang up. A real bank will happily wait ten minutes. A scammer will not.

Rule 3: Call back on a number you trust

Use the number printed on your card, on your passbook or inside your bank's official app. Never use a number that a caller or a search result gave you. For news and safety advice, you can also read the public pages of the Reserve Bank of India and NPCI, which runs UPI.

What genuine messages look like compared with scams

SignScamGenuine bank
ToneUrgent and threateningCalm, with time to respond
OTP or PINAsks for itNever asks for it
App or linkAsks you to install a new app or screen-sharePoints you to its own app
PaymentAsks for a "refundable" fee or depositDoes not ask you to pay to get your money

If you lose money: act in the first hour

Speed matters because the money moves quickly between accounts. If you have been defrauded, do these things in this order.

  1. Call the national cyber crime helpline, 1930, as soon as you can.
  2. Then file a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. If the helpline is busy, go straight to the portal.
  3. Call your bank, using the number on your card, and ask them to block the transaction and your card or UPI.
  4. Keep every screenshot, message, number and transaction ID. You will need them for the complaint.

Be realistic about the outcome. Reporting early gives you a better chance, but recovery is not guaranteed. That is why prevention matters more than any cure.

Report suspicious calls and messages before you lose money

You can also report a suspicious call, SMS or WhatsApp message before any damage happens. The Department of Telecommunications runs a facility called Chakshu on the Sanchar Saathi portal. You can report communication you received in the last 30 days. However, Chakshu is not for fraud that has already happened. For that, use 1930 and the cyber crime portal.

For students and first-time jobseekers

Young people face a particular kind of scam: the job that is too easy. A message offers good pay for liking videos, rating products or sending a few forms. Then it asks for a small "registration fee", or for a photo of your Aadhaar or PAN card to "verify" you.

  • A genuine employer never charges you a fee to hire you. If money has to leave your account before work begins, walk away.
  • Look for the company's own website, and check that the email on your offer letter matches its domain.
  • Share identity documents only after you have met the employer or verified them on an official channel. Never send them over a chat app to a stranger.
  • Talk to a teacher or an older relative before you pay anyone. Scammers hate a second opinion.

Money habits that make fraud less painful

Financial literacy and cyber safety go together. A few simple habits limit the damage if something goes wrong.

  • Keep only a small amount in the account you use for UPI. Save the rest in a separate account.
  • Set a daily transaction limit in your bank app, where the app allows it.
  • Check your account statement once a month, and ask about any payment you do not recognise.
  • Use a different password for your email than for any shopping site. Email is the key to your other accounts.

If you want to learn the wider basics of using the internet safely, the free Digital Literacy course on Vidaara is a good place to start. Students in Class 1 to 12 can also study for free on our Study page.

Frequently asked questions about online fraud in India

Can I get my money back after an online scam?

Sometimes, but nobody can promise it. Your best chance comes from acting fast. Call 1930, report on cybercrime.gov.in, and tell your bank straight away so it can try to hold the money before it moves on.

Does my bank ever ask for my OTP or PIN?

No genuine bank employee needs your OTP, card PIN, CVV or UPI PIN. If someone asks, treat the call as a scam, even if the caller knows your name or account number.

I only want to receive money by UPI. Do I need to enter my PIN?

No. You enter your UPI PIN only to send money. If a request says you must enter your PIN to receive money, it is a trick, so decline it.

What is Chakshu?

Chakshu is a facility on the Sanchar Saathi portal of the Department of Telecommunications. You can report suspicious calls, SMS or WhatsApp messages that you received in the last 30 days. It is for suspected fraud, not for money you have already lost.

How can I help my parents or grandparents stay safe?

Sit with them once and walk through the three rules in this guide. Agree on one family phone number they can call before they act on any urgent request. A two-minute call to a relative stops many scams.

posts.title: Hygiene Education for Children: Handwashing, Periods and Why Schools Need Both
posts.excerpt: A ten-minute handwashing lesson and an honest talk about periods can change how children grow up. Here is how to teach both, and what schools still need.
posts.meta_title: Hygiene Education for Children: A Practical Guide
posts.meta_desc: Hygiene education for children works best when it covers handwashing and menstrual health. Simple steps, honest limits and where to find help in India.
posts.cover_alt: A volunteer with school children at an Aagahi Foundation hygiene education session for children
posts.author: Aagahi Foundation

faqs.q: Why do children need soap, not just water?
faqs.a: Water alone removes some dirt, but soap breaks up the oils and germs that stick to skin. That is why health agencies recommend washing with soap. Rubbing your hands together for at least 20 seconds does most of the work.

faqs.q: How long should children wash their hands?
faqs.a: Scrub for at least 20 seconds, covering the palms, the backs of the hands, between the fingers and under the nails. A short song or a slow count to twenty helps younger children keep going.

faqs.q: When should we talk to a girl about periods?
faqs.a: Before they start. Many girls get their first period between about 10 and 15, so a calm conversation around age 9 or 10 is wise. Boys should hear about it too, so periods become normal rather than a secret.

faqs.q: Is it safe to use cloth during periods?
faqs.a: A clean pad is the safer choice where you can get one. If cloth is the only option, wash it with soap and water, dry it fully, preferably in sunlight, and store it in a clean place. Change it regularly through the day.

faqs.q: Where can adolescent girls get sanitary pads in India?
faqs.a: Under the Menstrual Hygiene Scheme, ASHA workers distribute subsidised pads, and some schools and anganwadi centres also supply them. Availability differs by state, so ask the local ASHA worker or health centre.

posts.content:
Hygiene education for children is not a single lesson about clean hands. It is a habit that grows over years, and it protects health, school attendance and dignity at the same time. The two topics that matter most, and that adults find hardest to talk about, are handwashing and menstrual health.

Aagahi Foundation runs hygiene sessions with school children and menstrual health conversations with women and girls in the community. This post shares practical advice for teaching both well, and it is honest about where good teaching still needs help from schools and governments.

Why handwashing is the best place to begin

Handwashing with soap is cheap, and the evidence for it is strong. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, washing hands with soap can cut diarrhoea among young children by roughly 30 per cent. The Global Handwashing Partnership repeats that figure. For a family where one sick day means a lost wage and a missed class, that is a big gain.

So start there. Every year on 15 October, Global Handwashing Day reminds schools around the world to do the same.

How to run a ten-minute handwashing lesson

Children learn by doing, not by listening. Keep the lesson short, and let every child practise.

  1. Wet your hands with clean water.
  2. Soap up and cover every part: palms, backs, between the fingers and under the nails.
  3. Scrub for at least 20 seconds. Count slowly, or sing a short song.
  4. Rinse well, then dry with a clean cloth or let your hands air dry.

Then teach the moments that matter most: after using the toilet, before eating, before cooking or serving food, and after playing outside or touching animals. The CDC's clean hands pages give a clear checklist you can print.

Menstrual health: start before the first period

Silence causes more harm than the period itself. Imagine a girl who has never heard about periods: she can feel frightened, and she may stay home from school. So a calm talk beforehand prevents most of that fear.

What should a good menstrual health session cover? These points matter most:

  • What a period is, in simple and truthful words, and that it is normal and healthy.
  • How to use a pad or clean cloth, and how often to change it through the day.
  • How to dispose of pads safely and privately, not in the toilet.
  • That myths about being "impure" are wrong. A girl can study, cook, play and pray as usual.

Boys and men belong in the conversation as well. When fathers, brothers and teachers understand periods, girls get more support and fewer jokes.

Myths that still hurt girls

Old beliefs travel quickly, and they shape how girls feel about their own bodies. Replace each one with a plain fact.

MythFact
A girl is "impure" during her period.A period is a normal body process. It has nothing to do with purity.
She must not cook, enter the kitchen or touch food.She can do all of these. Washing hands is enough.
She should skip school and sports.She can attend and play. Rest is fine if she feels unwell, but she does not need to hide.
Talking about periods is shameful.Silence is the real problem, because it keeps girls from asking for help.

Beyond hands: the other habits children need

Handwashing and menstrual health sit inside a bigger picture. Children also need a few other daily habits, and they are easy to teach together.

  • Safe drinking water. Use filtered or boiled water, and keep drinking containers covered.
  • Clean nails and hair. Trim nails every week. Short nails hold far less dirt.
  • Toilet use. Teach every child to use the toilet, to flush, and then to wash with soap.
  • Brushing teeth. Brush twice a day, and visit a health worker if a tooth hurts.
  • Clean food. Wash fruit and vegetables, and cover cooked food.

Where to find help in India

The Government of India runs a Menstrual Hygiene Scheme through the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. It began in 2011 as a pilot and now sits under the National Health Mission and the adolescent health programme. ASHA workers distribute subsidised pads to adolescent girls, and some schools and anganwadi centres supply them too. You can read about the programme on the National Health Mission site and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare site. Details and prices differ between states, so ask your local ASHA worker or health centre what is available near you.

The honest limit: lessons are not enough

Teaching only works when children can act on it. A child cannot wash with soap if the school has no running water. A girl cannot change a pad if the toilet has no door, no water and no bin.

If your school lacks these basics, raise it politely and in writing with the headmaster and the school management committee. Parents have more power here than they think. Meanwhile, we keep running sessions, because knowledge still helps even where facilities lag. However, we do not pretend that a talk replaces a working tap.

What parents and teachers can do this week

  • Put a bar of soap and a mug next to the household tap or the school water point.
  • Wash hands together before the midday meal, so children see adults doing it too.
  • Tell girls about periods before they start, and tell boys as well.
  • Ask your local ASHA worker or health centre about pads and other adolescent health services.

Children in Class 1 to 12 can also learn basic science, including health topics, for free on our Study page. You can see more of our school sessions in the Our work gallery.

Good hygiene education is patient work. One lesson will not change a habit, but a steady routine will. Repeat the same short steps every week, praise children who remember them, and let older students teach the younger ones. Children copy what they see, so the adults around them set the standard every day.

Frequently asked questions about hygiene education for children

Why do children need soap, not just water?

Water alone removes some dirt, but soap breaks up the oils and germs that stick to skin. That is why health agencies recommend washing with soap. Rubbing your hands together for at least 20 seconds does most of the work.

Before they start. Many girls get their first period between about 10 and 15, so a calm conversation around age 9 or 10 is wise. Boys should hear about it too, so periods become normal rather than a secret.

A clean pad is the safer choice where you can get one. If cloth is the only option, wash it with soap and water, dry it fully, preferably in sunlight, and store it in a clean place. Change it regularly through the day.

Under the Menstrual Hygiene Scheme, ASHA workers distribute subsidised pads, and some schools and anganwadi centres also supply them. Availability differs by state, so ask the local ASHA worker or health centre.

posts.title: Road Safety Awareness in India: Why We Take Street Plays to Busy Markets
posts.excerpt: India lost about 1.68 lakh lives on its roads in 2022. Here are the habits that protect riders and walkers, and what the law says about helping a crash victim.
posts.meta_title: Road Safety Awareness in India: Street Plays That Work
posts.meta_desc: Road safety awareness saves lives. See India's road death numbers, simple habits for riders and walkers, and what to do at a crash scene.
posts.cover_alt: Volunteers perform a street play on road safety awareness in a Delhi market with traffic police nearby
posts.author: Aagahi Foundation

faqs.q: Does a pillion rider also need a helmet?
faqs.a: Yes. The Motor Vehicles Act requires riders of two-wheelers, and their pillion passengers, to wear protective headgear that meets the Bureau of Indian Standards. A helmet only protects you when the strap is fastened.

faqs.q: If I help an accident victim, can the police trouble me?
faqs.a: The law protects you. Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act says a Good Samaritan who helps in good faith is not liable to civil or criminal action. A Good Samaritan who calls the police or takes the victim to hospital also cannot be forced to stay or answer unnecessary questions.

faqs.q: What is the golden hour?
faqs.a: The Motor Vehicles Act defines the golden hour as the first hour after a serious injury. During that hour, quick medical care gives the best chance of saving a life. That is why calling for help immediately matters so much.

faqs.q: Which number should I call after a crash?
faqs.a: Call 112, India's single emergency number, and ask for the police and an ambulance. Many states also run 108 for ambulances. Keep the line open and tell them the exact location.

faqs.q: What are the fines for traffic offences in Delhi?
faqs.a: Penalties change, so check the current official list rather than a blog. The Delhi Traffic Police website publishes the latest offences and amounts.

posts.content:
Road safety awareness is one of the few topics where a few minutes of attention can decide whether someone gets home. India recorded 4,61,312 road accidents in 2022, and 1,68,491 people died in them, according to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. Those numbers are families, not statistics.

Aagahi Foundation runs street-play road safety drives in busy Delhi markets, together with traffic police. This post explains why we choose street theatre, what the data says, and the habits that protect you and the people you love.

What the road safety numbers tell us

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways publishes the national figures each year. You can read its reports on the official MoRTH website. The 2022 report points to three things.

  • Riders pay the highest price. Two-wheeler users were the largest group among those killed, at roughly 75,000 people in 2022, according to press coverage of the report.
  • Speed is the biggest single cause. Overspeeding was linked to about seven in every ten road deaths.
  • Safety gear matters. A large number of the people killed were not wearing a helmet or a seat belt.

These figures come from the report as covered in the press, so please check the primary report before you quote an exact number.

Why we take road safety awareness to the street

A poster in a hallway does little, because people walk past it. A story in a busy market does more. When performers act out a near miss in costume and with humour, people stop. They watch because they are already waiting, and they remember the scene better than a rule.

Traffic police joined our drives in Delhi, and the press covered them. That matters, because commuters listen when the people who enforce the rules also explain the reasons.

Habits that protect riders

  1. Wear a BIS-standard helmet, and fasten the strap. A helmet on the head but not strapped offers very little protection.
  2. Insist that your pillion rider wears one too. The rule applies to them as well.
  3. Keep your speed within the limit, especially near schools, markets and crossings.
  4. Put your phone away. A text can wait. A crash cannot be undone.
  5. Never ride after drinking.

Drivers have their own list. Wear the seat belt in every seat, and secure children properly. Leave space between you and the vehicle ahead. Then slow down before a zebra crossing, not at it.

Habits that protect walkers and children

Pedestrians are not safe just because they are walking. Use the footpath and the zebra crossing wherever there is one. Stop at the kerb, look right, then left, then right again, and cross only when the road is clear. Teach children the same sequence, and practise it with them on a real road.

Never let a child run across the road to a parent or a friend. Hold hands near traffic until they can judge speed and distance themselves. That usually comes later than we expect.

The school run: small choices that matter

Every morning, millions of children travel to school on the back of a scooter or in a crowded vehicle. A few small choices lower the risk.

  • Never put three or more people on a two-wheeler. Overloaded bikes are hard to balance and brake.
  • Give a child a helmet that fits. An adult helmet slides around and protects little.
  • Seat young children in the back of a car, with a seat belt or a child restraint. Never hold a child on your lap.
  • Park a short walk away and let children step out on the footpath side, not into traffic.

How to start a road safety drive in your neighbourhood

You do not need a big budget to raise road safety awareness where you live. Start small and keep it simple.

  1. Pick one message, such as "wear your helmet" or "stop at the zebra crossing".
  2. Talk to the local traffic police and the market association first. Their support makes people listen.
  3. Keep the act short. Five minutes with a clear story and some humour holds a crowd better than a speech.
  4. End with one action. Ask everyone to try the habit this week, and thank them for stopping.

What to do if you see a crash

Most people hesitate because they fear trouble with the police. The law answers that fear directly. Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act protects a Good Samaritan who helps in good faith, and the rule grew out of a Supreme Court case brought by the SaveLIFE Foundation. In practice, here is what to do.

  1. Make yourself safe first. Switch on your hazard lights and stay clear of moving traffic.
  2. Call 112 and ask for the police and an ambulance. Give the exact place.
  3. Do not move the person unless there is immediate danger, such as fire. Moving someone with a neck or back injury can make it worse.
  4. Stay with them and keep them calm until help arrives.

The Act calls the first hour after a serious injury the "golden hour". Quick care in that hour gives the best chance of survival, so the call you make in the first minutes counts the most.

Know the rules where you live

Penalties and rules change, so do not rely on memory or on social media posts. The Delhi Traffic Police website lists current offences and challans. If you live in another state, check the traffic police site for your city.

If you want to bring a road safety session to your school, workplace or neighbourhood, contact us. You can also see more of our work in the Our work gallery, and young learners can study for free on our Study page.

Rules only work when people follow them even when nobody is watching. So the best habit you can build is the simplest one: treat every journey, short or long, as one that matters. Wear the helmet for the five-minute ride to the shop, too. Most crashes happen close to home, on roads we know well, and a moment of attention costs nothing.

Frequently asked questions about road safety awareness

Does a pillion rider also need a helmet?

Yes. The Motor Vehicles Act requires riders of two-wheelers, and their pillion passengers, to wear protective headgear that meets the Bureau of Indian Standards. A helmet only protects you when the strap is fastened.

If I help an accident victim, can the police trouble me?

The law protects you. Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act says a Good Samaritan who helps in good faith is not liable to civil or criminal action. A Good Samaritan who calls the police or takes the victim to hospital also cannot be forced to stay or answer unnecessary questions.

What is the golden hour?

The Motor Vehicles Act defines the golden hour as the first hour after a serious injury. During that hour, quick medical care gives the best chance of saving a life. That is why calling for help immediately matters so much.

Which number should I call after a crash?

Call 112, India's single emergency number, and ask for the police and an ambulance. Many states also run 108 for ambulances. Keep the line open and tell them the exact location.

What are the fines for traffic offences in Delhi?

Penalties change, so check the current official list rather than a blog. The Delhi Traffic Police website publishes the latest offences and amounts.

posts.title: The POSH Act Explained: Your Rights and Duties at Work in India
posts.excerpt: Every workplace in India has duties under the POSH Act. Here is what counts as harassment, who handles complaints, how long they take and where to go if there is no committee.
posts.meta_title: POSH Act Explained: Your Workplace Rights in India
posts.meta_desc: The POSH Act protects women from sexual harassment at work. Learn what counts, how an Internal Committee works, the time limits and how to complain.
posts.cover_alt: A speaker explains the POSH Act to a room of professionals at an Aagahi Foundation workshop
posts.author: Aagahi Foundation

faqs.q: Does the POSH Act protect men?
faqs.a: The Act protects women. Many employers also adopt gender-neutral policies, so ask your organisation about its own rules. A man who faces harassment may have other legal options, so it is wise to speak to a lawyer.

faqs.q: Does the Act cover interns, volunteers and contract staff?
faqs.a: Yes. The Act defines an employee broadly. It includes regular, temporary and daily-wage staff, contract workers, trainees, apprentices and people who work as volunteers, with or without pay.

faqs.q: How long do I have to file a complaint?
faqs.a: A written complaint should reach the committee within three months of the incident, or of the last incident in a series. The committee can extend that by another three months if it is satisfied that you had a good reason for the delay.

faqs.q: What if my workplace has no Internal Committee?
faqs.a: Employers with ten or more employees must have one. If yours does not, or you work for a smaller organisation, you can approach the Local Committee set up by the District Officer. The SHe-Box portal can also help you find the right committee.

faqs.q: Can a complaint be settled with money?
faqs.a: The Act allows conciliation, but only if the woman asks for it. It does not allow a money settlement as the basis for conciliation.

posts.content:
The POSH Act is the law that protects women from sexual harassment at work in India, yet many employees and even employers have never read it. POSH stands for the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013. It tells every workplace what it must do before a complaint arrives, and what it must do after.

Aagahi Foundation runs POSH awareness training for professionals. This post explains the Act in plain language. It is general information, not legal advice, so for a real case please speak to a lawyer or your Internal Committee.

Where the POSH Act came from

Before 2013, workplaces followed guidelines set by the Supreme Court in the Vishaka case of 1997. Parliament later turned those guidelines into a full law. You can read the Act on the India Code website, and the Ministry of Women and Child Development publishes official guidance.

What counts as sexual harassment under the POSH Act

The Act describes sexual harassment as any unwelcome behaviour of a sexual nature. That includes:

  • physical contact and advances,
  • a demand or request for sexual favours,
  • sexually coloured remarks,
  • showing pornography, and
  • any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature.

The key word is "unwelcome". It does not matter if the person meant it as a joke. What matters is how it affects the woman who received it.

Who is covered, and where

The word "workplace" is wide. It covers offices, shops, hospitals, schools, NGOs and government departments. It also covers places an employee visits for work, including transport that the employer provides. Even a domestic worker can complain.

The word "employee" is wide as well. Regular staff, daily-wage workers, contract workers, interns, trainees and volunteers all count.

The Internal Committee: who sits on it and what it does

Every workplace with ten or more employees must set up an Internal Committee, or IC. Each office or branch needs its own. The Act sets out who sits on it:

  • a senior woman employee as the presiding officer,
  • at least two members who are committed to women's causes or who have social work or legal experience,
  • one external member from an NGO or association working for women, or a person familiar with the issue, and
  • at least half of the members must be women.

The IC receives complaints, holds an inquiry, and recommends action to the employer. It should complete the inquiry within 90 days, and the Act requires it to keep the identities of everyone involved confidential.

If there is no Internal Committee

Smaller workplaces, with fewer than ten employees, do not need an IC. Instead, the District Officer sets up a Local Committee in each district. A woman can also go to the Local Committee if her complaint is against the employer. Either way, no one is left without a route.

The Ministry has also launched an online portal called SHe-Box. It helps women find the right committee and file a complaint, and it is meant to keep a record of committees across the country. Check the portal for the latest rules about registering committees.

How to file a complaint, step by step

  1. Write it down. Note the dates, places, what happened and who saw it. Keep messages, emails and any other evidence.
  2. Submit a written complaint to the Internal Committee or the Local Committee. If you cannot write it yourself, the committee must help you put it in writing.
  3. Do it within three months of the incident. The committee can extend this by three months for a good reason.
  4. Take part in the inquiry. Both sides can present their case.
  5. Expect an outcome. If the committee finds the complaint proved, it recommends action under the employer's service rules, such as a warning, a withheld promotion or termination.

Fear of retaliation stops many women from speaking up. If someone threatens your job because you complained, tell the committee in writing and speak to a lawyer.

Myths about the POSH Act

  • "It only applies to big companies." It does not. A small office with fewer than ten employees falls under the Local Committee instead, so the law still applies.
  • "It is only about a boss and an employee." The law covers harassment by anyone at work, including colleagues, clients and visitors.
  • "A joke cannot count." A joke can count if it is sexual and unwelcome. Intent does not decide the matter.
  • "Complaining will end my career." Many women fear that, and the fear is real. That is why the Act demands confidentiality and gives the committee power to recommend interim relief, such as a transfer or leave, while the inquiry runs.

How to support a colleague who has been harassed

Often the first person who hears about it is not a manager but a friend. If that is you, a few simple steps help.

  1. Listen without judging, and believe what you hear.
  2. Do not push her to complain, and do not pressure her to stay silent either. The choice is hers.
  3. Offer to help her write down the facts and keep the evidence.
  4. Tell her about the Internal Committee, and offer to go with her.
  5. Keep what she told you private.

What employers must do

An employer has duties even when no one has complained. It must set up an IC, display the penalties for harassment, hold awareness programmes, and give the IC the support it needs. That is exactly why training matters. A committee that nobody knows about cannot help anyone.

Frequently asked questions about the POSH Act

Does the POSH Act protect men?

The Act protects women. Many employers also adopt gender-neutral policies, so ask your organisation about its own rules. A man who faces harassment may have other legal options, so it is wise to speak to a lawyer.

Does the Act cover interns, volunteers and contract staff?

Yes. The Act defines an employee broadly. It includes regular, temporary and daily-wage staff, contract workers, trainees, apprentices and people who work as volunteers, with or without pay.

How long do I have to file a complaint?

A written complaint should reach the committee within three months of the incident, or of the last incident in a series. The committee can extend that by another three months if it is satisfied that you had a good reason for the delay.

What if my workplace has no Internal Committee?

Employers with ten or more employees must have one. If yours does not, or you work for a smaller organisation, you can approach the Local Committee set up by the District Officer. The SHe-Box portal can also help you find the right committee.

Can a complaint be settled with money?

The Act allows conciliation, but only if the woman asks for it. It does not allow a money settlement as the basis for conciliation.
